subject: biology
title: Translation
summary: How the genetic code is read by transfer RNA and the ribosome to build a protein, and how proteins are changed afterwards.

concepts.name: Genetic code
concepts.summary: The table of three-nucleotide codons, each naming one amino acid or a stop signal, that cells use to read mRNA.

explain.text: The genetic code is the table that matches each three-nucleotide codon in mRNA to an amino acid or to a stop signal. Cells read a gene three letters at a time, so the 64 possible codons cover the 20 amino acids that proteins use. Three codons are stop signals, and AUG is the usual start, which also codes for methionine. Most amino acids have more than one codon, so the code is degenerate. Almost every organism uses the same table, so a bacterium and a person read the same codon the same way.

misconceptions.claim: One nucleotide codes for one amino acid.
misconceptions.correction: A codon is three nucleotides. Four bases read one at a time give only four signals, too few for 20 amino acids. Read three at a time they give 64.

misconceptions.claim: Each amino acid has exactly one codon.
misconceptions.correction: Most amino acids have two to six codons. Because the code is degenerate, different codons can name the same amino acid.

misconceptions.claim: Each species has its own genetic code.
misconceptions.correction: The code is nearly universal: the same codon names the same amino acid in nearly all life. Rare exceptions exist, such as in some mitochondria.

concepts.name: Transfer RNA
concepts.summary: A small RNA that carries one amino acid to the ribosome, using an anticodon to pair with the matching mRNA codon.

explain.text: Transfer RNA, or tRNA, is a small RNA that carries one amino acid to the ribosome. Each tRNA has an anticodon, three bases that pair with a matching codon on the mRNA, and an attachment site at its other end for one amino acid. An enzyme, aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase, loads each tRNA with the right amino acid before it is used. The loaded form is called an aminoacyl-tRNA. The ribosome reads the pairing and joins the carried amino acid to the growing chain.

misconceptions.claim: Each amino acid has just one tRNA.
misconceptions.correction: Many amino acids have several tRNAs, which differ in their anticodons. Each tRNA still carries one amino acid.

misconceptions.claim: The ribosome attaches the amino acid to the tRNA.
misconceptions.correction: An aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase, an enzyme, attaches each amino acid to its matching tRNA before the ribosome uses it.

misconceptions.claim: The anticodon is the same sequence as the codon.
misconceptions.correction: The anticodon pairs with the codon, so it is complementary to it, and the two run in opposite directions.

concepts.name: Translation
concepts.summary: The ribosome reads mRNA codon by codon and joins the amino acids carried by tRNAs into a polypeptide chain.

explain.text: Translation builds a protein from an mRNA sequence. A ribosome in the cytoplasm reads the mRNA codon by codon and moves along it. Each aminoacyl-tRNA whose anticodon pairs with the codon enters the A site, a peptide bond forms, and the ribosome shifts one codon. Translation starts at an AUG start codon and ends when a stop codon is read and a release factor frees the finished chain. Several ribosomes can read one mRNA at once, so many copies of a protein can be made quickly.

misconceptions.claim: Translation happens inside the nucleus, along with transcription.
misconceptions.correction: Translation happens on ribosomes in the cytoplasm, outside the nucleus. Transcription, which makes the mRNA, happens in the nucleus.

misconceptions.claim: New amino acids join at the start of the chain.
misconceptions.correction: Each new amino acid joins the carboxyl end, so the chain grows from its amino end toward its carboxyl end.

misconceptions.claim: An mRNA is read by one ribosome at a time.
misconceptions.correction: Several ribosomes can read one mRNA at once, following one another along it. The group is called a polyribosome.

concepts.name: Post-translational modification
concepts.summary: Changes made to a protein after translation, such as adding phosphate or sugar groups or cutting the chain, which alter what it does.

explain.text: After translation, many proteins are changed before they work. Enzymes can add a phosphate group, which can switch an enzyme on or off, or a sugar chain, which can help a protein fold and direct it to the right place. Some proteins are also cut by proteases into shorter, active forms. These changes alter the protein, not the gene: the DNA sequence stays the same. A protein's final shape and activity depend on its amino acid sequence and on what is added or cut afterwards.

misconceptions.claim: The amino acid sequence fixes everything about a protein, so nothing changes after translation.
misconceptions.correction: Many proteins are changed after translation by adding groups such as phosphate or sugar, or by cutting the chain. These changes alter how the protein works.

misconceptions.claim: Changing a protein after translation changes the gene.
misconceptions.correction: A modification changes only the protein. The DNA sequence stays the same, so the gene is not altered.

misconceptions.claim: Modifications are cosmetic and do not affect what a protein does.
misconceptions.correction: Phosphorylation can switch an enzyme on or off, and sugar chains affect how a protein folds and where it goes.

items.prompt: How many nucleotides make up one codon?
choices: One
Two
Three
Sixteen
items.explanation: A codon is three nucleotides. Three bases give 64 combinations, enough for the 20 amino acids. One base gives 4 signals, and two bases give only 16, which is still too few for 20 amino acids.

items.prompt: How many codons does the genetic code have, counting the three stop codons?
items.explanation: Four bases in each of three positions give 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 codons. Of these, 61 name amino acids and three are stop signals. The number 20 is the count of amino acids, not of codons.

items.prompt: A student says: each amino acid has exactly one codon, so any change to a codon must change the protein. What is wrong with that?
choices: Each codon names one amino acid, so every codon change alters the protein
A codon has four nucleotides, so one change shifts every later codon
Several codons can name the same amino acid, so some changes leave it the same
The ribosome repairs a changed codon before reading it, so the protein stays the same
items.explanation: The premise is false: most amino acids have two to six codons, so some single-base changes swap one codon for a synonym and leave the amino acid unchanged. Ribosomes do not repair codons.

items.prompt: Which amino acid does the start codon AUG normally code for?
choices: Methionine
Glycine
Tryptophan
Lysine
items.explanation: AUG is the usual start codon, and it codes for methionine, so new proteins begin with methionine, which may be removed later. Glycine, tryptophan and lysine each have their own codons, none of them AUG.

items.prompt: Which statement about the stop codons UAA, UAG and UGA is correct?
choices: Each one is read by a tRNA that carries a specific amino acid
Each one ends translation, and no amino acid is added for it
Each one marks the start of translation, so it is read first
Each one codes for an amino acid that is found at the end of a protein
items.explanation: Release factors, not tRNAs, recognise the three stop codons, and the finished chain is released with no amino acid added. Stop codons mark the end; AUG is the usual start.

items.prompt: A bacterial gene and a human gene each code for a protein. Which statement about the genetic code they share is most accurate?
choices: Each species has its own code, so the same codon names different amino acids in each
The same codon names the same amino acid in nearly all life, with rare exceptions
The code differs inside the nucleus, so the two genes cannot be compared
Bacteria read codons of two nucleotides and humans read codons of three
items.explanation: The genetic code is nearly universal. The rare exceptions, such as some mitochondrial codons, do not change the general rule. A student who thinks each species has its own table would pick the claim that the codons differ between species.

items.prompt: A human gene is put into bacteria, which then make the correct human protein from it. What does this show?
choices: The same codons name the same amino acids in both, so the message is read alike
The human gene is first converted into a bacterial code, so the amino acids match by design
Bacteria and humans use different codons, and the amino acids match by chance
The bacteria copy the human ribosome, so they translate the gene directly
items.explanation: The protein is correct because the codons name the same amino acids in both organisms. A student who holds that each species has its own code would call the match a coincidence.

items.prompt: A DNA change turns the codon GAA into GAG. Both codons name glutamate. What is the effect on the protein at that position?
choices: The protein gets a different amino acid at that position
The protein stops early, because the new codon is a stop codon
None: glutamate is still added, so the amino acid sequence is unchanged
The ribosome skips that codon, so the protein is one amino acid shorter
items.explanation: Glutamate has two codons, GAA and GAG, so this change is silent: the same amino acid goes into the chain. A student who thinks each amino acid has one codon would expect a different amino acid here.

items.prompt: Why does the genetic code read nucleotides three at a time rather than one at a time?
choices: Each base alone is one amino acid, so one base per codon would be enough
Three bases are needed to attach the amino acid to the ribosome
Three bases give 64 combinations, enough for 20 amino acids
A codon of three bases is the length of one tRNA molecule
items.explanation: With four bases, one base gives 4 signals and two bases give 16, both too few for 20 amino acids. Three bases give 64, which leaves room for every amino acid with some codons to spare.

items.prompt: A mutation changes a codon in the middle of a gene into UAA, a stop codon. What is the most likely result?
choices: Translation ends early at that codon, and a shorter protein is made
The new stop codon is skipped, so the protein keeps its full length
Translation continues, with the amino acid there replaced by a different one
The mRNA breaks down in the nucleus before it reaches the ribosome
items.explanation: A stop codon ends the chain, so every codon after the mutation is lost and the protein is shorter. Stop codons are read by release factors, not skipped, and the mRNA is not destroyed by this change.

items.prompt: A tRNA's anticodon is GAA, written 5′ to 3′. Which mRNA codon, also written 5′ to 3′, does it pair with?
choices: UUC
GAA
CUU
AAG
items.explanation: The strands pair antiparallel, with A pairing with U and G with C. GAA reads as UUC in the mRNA. Writing the same letters, GAA, is the mistake of thinking the anticodon and codon are identical.

items.prompt: Which part of a tRNA pairs with the codon on the mRNA?
choices: The anticodon
The amino acid attachment site
The 5′ cap
The poly-A tail
items.explanation: The anticodon is three bases that pair with a codon. The attachment site holds the amino acid, and the 5′ cap and poly-A tail belong to mRNA, not to tRNA.

items.prompt: Which enzyme attaches each amino acid to its matching tRNA?
choices: Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase
The ribosome, as it reads the mRNA
RNA polymerase
DNA ligase
items.explanation: Each aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase matches one amino acid to its tRNA and makes the bond. The ribosome uses charged tRNAs but does not load them, and RNA polymerase and DNA ligase do other jobs.

items.prompt: What is an aminoacyl-tRNA?
choices: A tRNA with its amino acid attached
An mRNA codon with an amino acid attached
A ribosome subunit that holds an amino acid
A tRNA with its anticodon removed
items.explanation: An aminoacyl-tRNA is a tRNA that has been charged with its own amino acid, ready to be delivered to the ribosome. Codons and ribosome subunits are not tRNAs, and a tRNA without its anticodon could not pair with a codon.

items.prompt: Why can one amino acid be carried by several different tRNAs?
choices: Each tRNA carries two amino acids, so one amino acid needs several
Different codons for one amino acid need tRNAs with different anticodons
Each amino acid has just one tRNA, and the rest are copies made by mistake
The ribosome uses up tRNAs, so the cell has to make many copies of them
items.explanation: An amino acid can have several codons, and each codon pairs with a tRNA that has a matching anticodon. A tRNA carries one amino acid, and tRNAs are reused rather than used up.

items.prompt: A student says: each amino acid has exactly one tRNA, so one tRNA can read every codon for that amino acid. What is wrong with that?
choices: The student is right, because one tRNA carries each amino acid
Many amino acids have several tRNAs, each with its own anticodon
A tRNA can carry any amino acid, so the number of tRNAs does not matter
The cell makes tRNAs in the nucleus, so it has just one kind
items.explanation: Many amino acids have several codons, and each codon can need a tRNA with a different anticodon. One tRNA carries one amino acid, but a single tRNA cannot pair with every codon for it.

items.prompt: Put these steps in order, from start to finish, for loading an amino acid onto its tRNA.
steps: The enzyme binds the correct amino acid and ATP, and activates the amino acid
The activated amino acid is transferred onto the 3′ end of its matching tRNA
The charged tRNA is released, ready to carry its amino acid to the ribosome
items.explanation: The synthetase first binds and activates the amino acid, then passes it to the tRNA. The charged tRNA is released only after the bond is made, so the order cannot be swapped.

items.prompt: A tRNA is loaded with lysine, but its anticodon is changed so that it pairs with a codon for phenylalanine. What happens to the protein?
choices: Phenylalanine is placed at lysine codons, and lysine at phenylalanine codons
Lysine is placed at phenylalanine codons, so the protein is wrong there
Nothing changes, because the amino acid is chosen by the anticodon
The ribosome rejects the tRNA, so translation stops at that codon
items.explanation: The synthetase sets the amino acid when it loads the tRNA, so the anticodon does not choose it. Pairing with a phenylalanine codon puts lysine there. The ribosome checks the anticodon pairing, not the amino acid carried, so the error reaches the protein.

items.prompt: A cell lacks the enzyme that attaches amino acids to tRNAs. What is the most likely effect on translation?
choices: The ribosome attaches amino acids to tRNAs itself, so translation runs normally
Uncharged tRNAs cannot deliver amino acids, so the protein chain cannot grow
The tRNAs still arrive charged from the cytoplasm, so translation is unaffected
The mRNA is read backwards, so the protein is made from its end
items.explanation: Without the synthetase, tRNAs stay uncharged, so no amino acid reaches the A site and the chain stops growing. The ribosome reads the codon and joins amino acids, but it does not load the tRNAs.

items.prompt: Why is an anticodon described as complementary to its codon?
choices: It has the same bases as the codon, so the two match letter for letter
It pairs with the codon by base pairing, in the opposite direction
It is made of amino acids that match the letters of the codon
It is a copy of the amino acid that the codon names
items.explanation: A pairs with U and G with C, and the two strands run in opposite directions. Identical sequences would not pair with each other, so the match is complementary, not identical.

items.prompt: Where in a eukaryotic cell does translation take place?
choices: In the nucleus, alongside transcription
On ribosomes in the cytoplasm
Inside the lysosome
On the outer surface of the cell membrane
items.explanation: Translation happens on ribosomes in the cytoplasm, outside the nucleus. Transcription, which makes the mRNA, happens in the nucleus, so placing translation there mixes up the two steps.

items.prompt: Where is each new amino acid joined onto a growing polypeptide?
choices: At the carboxyl (C) end of the chain
At the amino (N) end of the chain
At a random point along the chain
At the 5′ end of the mRNA molecule, where it begins
items.explanation: Each new amino acid joins the carboxyl end, so the chain grows from its amino end toward its carboxyl end. The amino end is where the chain starts, not where new amino acids are added.

items.prompt: Why do cells often have several ribosomes reading one mRNA at the same time?
choices: A single ribosome can read an mRNA at a time, so extra ribosomes waste energy
Each ribosome reads a different gene on the same mRNA
Many copies of the protein can be made quickly from one mRNA
The first ribosome uses up the mRNA, so others take over its job
items.explanation: Ribosomes follow one another along the same mRNA, so one message makes many protein copies at once. A student who holds that one ribosome at a time is the rule would call the extra ribosomes wasteful.

items.prompt: Which codon is the usual start of translation?
choices: AUG
UAA
UAG
UGA
items.explanation: AUG is the usual start codon, and it codes for methionine. UAA, UAG and UGA are the three stop codons, which end translation.

items.prompt: In elongation, what happens right after a peptide bond forms between two amino acids?
choices: The ribosome moves one codon, so the next codon sits in the A site
The ribosome slides back to the start codon and starts over
The finished chain is released, and the ribosome splits into subunits
The mRNA is copied again from the gene before the next amino acid joins
items.explanation: After the peptide bond, translocation moves the ribosome one codon along the mRNA, shifting the tRNAs into the P and E sites and opening the A site for the next aminoacyl-tRNA. Release and splitting happen only at the end.

items.prompt: A ribosome reaches a UAG stop codon in its A site. What binds to the A site next?
choices: A tRNA carrying the amino acid that UAG usually codes for
A release factor, which triggers the chain to be freed
A tRNA carrying the last amino acid of the chain
The start codon's methionine tRNA, which restarts translation
items.explanation: tRNAs do not recognise stop codons. A release factor binds the stop codon, and the ribosome releases the finished chain. A stop codon codes for no amino acid, so no tRNA carries one for it.

items.prompt: In bacteria, ribosomes often start reading an mRNA before it is fully made. Why is that possible?
choices: Transcription and translation both happen in the nucleus, so they can overlap
Bacteria have no nucleus, so transcription and translation share the cytoplasm
Bacterial ribosomes wait until the whole gene has been copied before they begin
Bacterial mRNA is made inside the ribosome, so reading starts at once
items.explanation: Without a nuclear membrane, a bacterium's mRNA is still being made when ribosomes attach to its free end, so the two processes overlap. In eukaryotes the mRNA is made in the nucleus and exported first.

items.prompt: A mutation stops release factors from binding stop codons. What is the most likely result for a gene that normally ends with a stop codon?
choices: Translation stops one codon early, and a shorter protein is made
Translation runs past the stop codon, making a longer protein
The stop codon is skipped without any change in the protein
The ribosome falls off the mRNA before the start codon is reached
items.explanation: Without release at the stop codon, the ribosome keeps adding amino acids until it meets another stop codon, so the protein is longer. Stopping early would need a stop codon to be read sooner.

items.prompt: Several ribosomes read one mRNA, spaced along it. Which ribosome has made the longest chain so far?
choices: The one nearest the 3′ end, which started reading earliest
The one nearest the 5′ end, which started reading last
A single ribosome reads an mRNA at a time, so that one has made the longest chain
All of them have made chains of the same length
items.explanation: Ribosomes start at the 5′ end and move toward the 3′ end, so the one furthest along started earliest and has the longest chain. Ribosomes at different points along the mRNA have chains of different lengths.

items.prompt: During elongation, which ribosome site holds the tRNA that carries the growing chain?
choices: The A site
The P site
The E site
The stop site
items.explanation: The P (peptidyl) site holds the tRNA whose amino acid is part of the growing chain. The A site receives the next aminoacyl-tRNA, and the E site is where empty tRNAs leave.

items.prompt: Put the stages of translation in order, from start to finish.
steps: Initiation: the small subunit and start tRNA assemble on the start codon
Elongation: amino acids are added one codon at a time
Termination: a stop codon is reached and a release factor frees the chain
Recycling: the ribosome splits into subunits so they can be reused
items.explanation: Translation starts with initiation, adds amino acids during elongation, ends at a stop codon, and then the ribosome is recycled. Recycling comes last because the subunits are only free once the chain is released.

items.prompt: Put these events of one elongation cycle in order, from start to finish.
steps: A tRNA carrying the matching amino acid enters the A site
A peptide bond forms, moving the chain onto the tRNA in the A site
The ribosome moves one codon, shifting the tRNAs into the P and E sites
The empty tRNA leaves from the E site, and the A site is free again
items.explanation: The incoming tRNA must arrive first, the bond forms next, the ribosome then shifts, and the empty tRNA leaves last. Each step depends on the one before it.

items.prompt: Which statement about how a polypeptide grows during translation is correct?
choices: It grows by adding amino acids to its carboxyl end
It grows by adding amino acids to its amino end
It grows from both of its ends at the same time
It grows only after a stop codon is read, all at once
items.explanation: Each amino acid is joined to the carboxyl end of the chain, so the chain lengthens there. Growth at both ends, or a single burst after a stop codon, does not happen.

items.prompt: Which small group do kinases most often add to a protein?
choices: A phosphate group
A sugar chain
A lipid tail
An extra amino acid
items.explanation: Kinases transfer a phosphate group, usually from ATP, onto specific amino acids of a protein. Sugar chains and lipid tails are added by other enzymes, and an extra amino acid would need a new codon in the gene.

items.prompt: Which modification shortens a protein by cutting its backbone?
choices: Proteolytic cleavage, a cut through peptide bonds
Glycosylation, which adds sugar chains to the protein
Phosphorylation, which adds a phosphate group
Ubiquitination, which tags a protein for removal
items.explanation: Proteases cut peptide bonds, which removes or activates part of a chain. Glycosylation adds sugars, phosphorylation adds a phosphate, and ubiquitination attaches a small protein tag.

items.prompt: Which class of enzyme adds phosphate groups to proteins?
choices: Kinases
Ligases
Polymerases
Ribozymes
items.explanation: Kinases transfer phosphate groups onto proteins. Ligases join pieces together, polymerases copy nucleic acids, and ribozymes are RNA molecules that catalyse reactions.

items.prompt: A kinase adds a phosphate to an enzyme, and the enzyme becomes active. What does this show?
choices: A protein's activity can be switched by a change that alters its shape or charge
The enzyme's activity is fixed by its amino acid sequence, so the phosphate has no effect
The phosphate changes the gene, so the next copy of the enzyme is active
The phosphate is a sugar that changes which codon the enzyme reads
items.explanation: A phosphate group carries negative charge and changes the protein's shape, so the protein's activity can be switched. The sequence does not fix activity by itself, and the gene is not changed by a phosphate.

items.prompt: A protein is phosphorylated after translation. What does that mean for the gene that encoded the protein?
choices: The gene is unchanged, and only the protein carries the phosphate
The gene now carries a phosphate and passes it to each new copy
The gene's codons change, so the next protein has a different sequence
The gene is switched off for good, so the protein can never be made again
items.explanation: The phosphate is added to the finished protein by an enzyme. The DNA sequence and its codons are not changed, so the next copy of the gene makes the same protein before any modification.

items.prompt: Glycosylation adds sugar chains to some proteins. What is a main job of those chains?
choices: They help a protein fold and direct it to its destination
They replace the amino acids that the codons name
They are cosmetic and leave what the protein does unchanged
They make the protein's gene copy itself faster
items.explanation: Sugar chains added in the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi help proteins fold and act as address labels for sorting. They do not replace amino acids, and they do not act on the gene.

items.prompt: A cell switches an enzyme off by adding a phosphate. Which statement describes what changed?
choices: The enzyme's activity changed, with no change to its gene
The enzyme was destroyed, so it cannot be used again
The enzyme's amino acid sequence was rewritten by the phosphate
The enzyme was switched off by a change in its codons
items.explanation: Phosphorylation changed the enzyme's activity while leaving its gene and amino acid sequence intact. Phosphate can be removed again, so the enzyme is not destroyed.

items.prompt: A student says a protein's function is set by its amino acid sequence alone, so nothing added later can change it. What is the best reply?
choices: Later changes such as phosphorylation can switch the protein's activity on or off
The sequence is enough, because the ribosome reads the final function from the codons
Changes to DNA alone decide a protein's function, so the student is right
Proteins are fixed once they are made, so the student is right
items.explanation: Modifications added after translation can switch a protein's activity, so the sequence alone does not decide function. The ribosome reads codons but does not set final activity, and the DNA is not what changes the protein.

items.prompt: A protein made by translation is cut by a protease, and the cut piece is the active form. Which idea does this illustrate?
choices: A modification by cutting can be needed before a protein is active
Cutting is cosmetic and leaves what the protein does unchanged
The cut changes the codons, so the next copy of the protein is shorter
Cutting happens in bacteria, where ribosomes make shorter chains
items.explanation: Here the cut is what switches the protein on, so modification after translation can be required for activity. The gene is not changed by a cut, and cutting happens in many organisms, not only bacteria.

items.prompt: Put these steps in order, from start to finish, for a protein that is secreted from the cell.
steps: The ribosome makes the polypeptide from the mRNA's codons
A signal sequence at the chain's start guides it into the endoplasmic reticulum
Enzymes in the endoplasmic reticulum add sugar chains to the protein
Vesicles carry the modified protein on toward the Golgi apparatus
items.explanation: The chain is made first, then guided into the endoplasmic reticulum, where sugars are added, and only then packed into vesicles for the Golgi. Sugar addition needs the chain to be inside the endoplasmic reticulum.

verification.note: b's note: Signal-sequence targeting is co-translational, so steps 2 and 3 overlap somewhat; order chosen by chain start then ER entry.

items.prompt: Tap the tRNA that has just brought in the next amino acid to be added to the chain.
items.explanation: The A site takes in each new aminoacyl-tRNA. Its anticodon pairs with the codon there, and it carries one amino acid that will join the chain.

items.prompt: Tap the tRNA that is holding the growing polypeptide.
items.explanation: The tRNA in the P site holds the chain made so far. When a peptide bond forms, the chain passes to the amino acid on the A-site tRNA.

items.prompt: Tap the tRNA that has handed over its chain and is about to leave the ribosome.
items.explanation: After the ribosome moves on, the tRNA that gave up its chain sits in the E site, carrying nothing, and then leaves to be loaded again.

items.prompt: Tap the molecule whose codons decide which amino acid comes next.
items.explanation: The mRNA runs between the two subunits. Its codons are read three bases at a time, and each one is matched by a tRNA anticodon.

items.prompt: Tap the part of the ribosome that joins amino acids with peptide bonds.
items.explanation: The large subunit catalyses the peptide bond between the chain on the P-site tRNA and the amino acid on the A-site tRNA.

items.prompt: Tap the ribosome subunit that binds the mRNA first when translation begins.
items.explanation: The small subunit binds the mRNA and finds the start codon with the initiator tRNA. The large subunit joins afterwards.

items.prompt: Tap the three tRNA bases that pair with a codon.
items.explanation: The anticodon is three bases in the bottom loop of the tRNA. They pair with a complementary codon in the mRNA.

items.prompt: Tap the three mRNA bases that name the amino acid this tRNA brings.
items.explanation: A codon is three mRNA bases read together. The tRNA whose anticodon pairs with them brings the matching amino acid.

items.prompt: Tap the arm of the tRNA where aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase attaches the amino acid.
items.explanation: The amino acid is joined to the end of the acceptor stem, at the opposite end of the tRNA from the anticodon.

items.prompt: Tap what this charged tRNA delivers to the ribosome.
items.explanation: A charged tRNA carries one amino acid on its acceptor end. At the ribosome that amino acid is added to the growing chain.

artifacts.title: A ribosome during elongation
artifacts.alt: A side view of a ribosome on an mRNA strand. A small sand-coloured subunit lies under the mRNA and a large pale blue-grey subunit sits above it. Three tRNAs stand side by side in the large subunit: a tilted sage one on the left, lifting away from the mRNA with nothing attached; a dark green one in the middle, paired to its codon and holding a chain of beads that leaves through the top of the ribosome; and an ochre one on the right, paired to the next codon and carrying a single bead.

artifacts.title: A charged tRNA reading a codon
artifacts.alt: A tRNA drawn flat as a cloverleaf: a paired stem at the top, a looped arm to each side, and a looped arm at the bottom. One strand runs past the top stem and curves to a sand-coloured ball. Three red bases on the bottom loop face three ochre bases in a long blue-grey mRNA strand below, joined by dotted lines.

artifacts.title: One round of elongation
artifacts.alt: Six steps: the ribosome reads a codon of the mRNA, a matching charged tRNA enters the A site, the large subunit joins the chain to the new amino acid, the ribosome moves one codon so that tRNA sits in the P site, the empty tRNA leaves from the E site, and the chain grows by one amino acid.

steps.title: Read the next codon
steps.text: The ribosome holds the mRNA and exposes one codon at a time in its A site.

steps.title: A charged tRNA arrives
steps.text: A tRNA whose anticodon pairs with that codon enters the A site, carrying one amino acid.

steps.title: A peptide bond forms
steps.text: The large subunit moves the chain from the P-site tRNA onto the amino acid of the A-site tRNA, joining them with a peptide bond.

steps.title: The ribosome moves on
steps.text: The ribosome shifts one codon along the mRNA, so the tRNA holding the chain now sits in the P site.

steps.title: The empty tRNA leaves
steps.text: The tRNA that gave up its chain moves to the E site and leaves the ribosome, ready to be loaded again.

steps.title: The chain grows
steps.text: The polypeptide is one amino acid longer and threads out of the large subunit. The cycle repeats until a stop codon.
